how-much-sleep-do-kids-need-by-age:
Sleep is the single variable that changes most about the following day, and it is the one most often traded away. Here are the ranges, and then the part that matters more than the ranges.

AgeTotal in 24 hoursNotes
1 to 211 to 14 hoursIncluding one nap for most
3 to 510 to 13 hoursNaps usually stop somewhere in here
6 to 129 to 12 hoursThe range narrows in practice; most need the upper half
13 to 188 to 10 hoursBody clock shifts later. This is biology, not laziness

Short sleep does not look like tiredness

This is the part worth knowing. An adult who is short of sleep looks sleepy. A child who is short of sleep looks fidgety, silly, irritable and unable to settle. It reads as behaviour, so it gets treated as behaviour, and the actual cause goes unexamined for months.

Before treating a concentration or behaviour problem as what it appears to be, count the hours honestly for a week. Not what time they went up: what time they actually fell asleep, and what time they woke.

What matters as much as the total

Consistency. A regular sleep and wake time, including weekends within an hour or so, matters nearly as much as duration. Wildly different weekend timings produce a Monday that is genuinely harder for physiological reasons.

The hour before. Screens, bright light and anything exciting delay sleep onset. The mechanism is more about arousal and displaced hours than blue light alone, which is why a calm boring hour beats a filter.

Where the device sleeps. No screens in bedrooms overnight is the most evidence-supported rule in this whole area and the one most worth holding.

Teenagers

Adolescent body clocks genuinely shift later at puberty. A fourteen-year-old who cannot fall asleep at ten is not being difficult; their melatonin is arriving later than yours. Combined with early school starts this produces a chronic shortfall that they then try to repay at weekends, which shifts the clock further.

The practical levers are morning light, a consistent wake time, and getting the phone out of the room. Arguing about bedtime is the least effective of the available options.

When to ask

Loud snoring, pauses in breathing, or mouth breathing every night are worth mentioning to a doctor rather than treated as a sleep habit. So is a child who is getting adequate hours and is still exhausted.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for advice from a doctor who knows your child.
how-much-physical-activity-do-kids-need:
The usual answer is an hour a day of moderate to vigorous activity for children over five, with under-fives needing considerably more and mostly through play. That number is a reasonable target and it is not the interesting part.

The interesting part is that movement is not primarily about fitness at this age. It is doing developmental work that nothing else does, and understanding which work changes what you optimise for.

What movement is actually building

Attention. Children generally settle to a demanding task better after movement than before it. The effect is short-lived and real, which is an argument for movement before homework rather than as a reward after it.

Sleep. Physically tired children fall asleep faster and sleep more deeply, and sleep then improves attention and mood. This is the most reliable chain in the whole area.

The trunk and shoulders. Climbing, hanging and carrying build the stability that later steadies a hand for writing. A child who cannot sit comfortably cannot write comfortably, and the fix is at the shoulder rather than the pencil.

Risk calibration. A child who has climbed and occasionally fallen has information about heights that cannot be told to them. Removing all risk removes the learning as well as the bruise.

Mood. The association between activity and lower rates of anxiety and low mood in children is consistent, though the direction is not always clean.

What counts

Almost everything except sitting. Walking to school, running about at break, carrying shopping, climbing a tree, dancing in the kitchen, a scooter, chasing a sibling. It does not have to be a sport and it does not have to be organised, and for younger children unorganised is generally better because it includes more variety of movement.

Three kinds are worth having across a week: something that raises the heart rate, something that loads muscle and bone such as climbing or jumping, and something that involves balance and coordination.

The organised sport question

Useful for many children and not required. A weekly hour of football is less movement than daily walking and free play, and early specialisation in one sport is associated with more overuse injury and more dropping out rather than better outcomes. Variety is the better bet until well into adolescence.

The easiest lever in most households

Not adding an activity. Removing a car journey, going outside for twenty minutes after school before anything else happens, and letting the walk to somewhere be the activity rather than the obstacle before it.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for advice from a doctor who knows your child.
how-screen-time-affects-childrens-sleep:
The blue light explanation is the one everybody knows and it is the smaller half of the story. The larger half is simpler and more actionable.

Three mechanisms, in order of how much they matter

Displacement. The hour spent on a screen is an hour not spent asleep. This is the biggest effect by some distance and it requires no biology to explain: bedtime moves later, wake time does not, and the shortfall accumulates across a week.

Arousal. What is on the screen matters more than the screen. A game with stakes, a group chat, an argument in a comment thread or a cliffhanger episode leaves a child alert and thinking. A dull programme does not. This is why "screens before bed" is too blunt a rule to be useful: half an hour of something calm and half an hour of competitive gaming are not the same intervention.

Light. Real, and smaller than the others. Bright light in the evening does delay melatonin. The effect from a phone at typical distances is modest compared with displacement, which is why night-shift filters produce disappointing results in studies: they address the smallest mechanism and leave the other two intact.

What the evidence supports

The association between evening screen use and shorter, later, poorer sleep in children is one of the more consistent findings in this contested area. What is less clear is size and direction: some of it is likely to be children who sleep badly reaching for a device, rather than the device causing the poor sleep.

What is not contested is the device in the bedroom overnight. That association is strong, it survives adjustment for other factors, and it is the single rule most worth holding.

What actually works

Charge devices outside bedrooms. One place, all devices, adults included. This solves the problem structurally rather than by trust, and it removes the two in the morning scroll as well as the midnight one.

Set a stop time, not a limit. "Screens off at eight" is enforceable and needs no adjudication. "An hour a day" requires a negotiation every day.

Care what it is, not just when. Move the stimulating things earlier in the evening and let the last stretch be dull.

Fix mornings too. Morning daylight anchors the body clock, and it is the most underused lever available with teenagers.

Teenagers specifically

Their clock has genuinely shifted later at puberty, so they are fighting biology before any phone is involved. Add a group chat that is most active at eleven at night and the shortfall is structural. The phone out of the room does more here than any other single change, and it is worth a difficult fortnight to establish.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for advice from a doctor who knows your child.
sensory-activities-for-kids-at-home:
Sensory play is often presented as something for children with sensory difficulties. It is for all of them, and it is worth understanding what each kind of input actually does before setting any of it up, because the choice is not arbitrary.

The two senses nobody was taught about

Most people can name five. Two more do most of the regulating work and neither is well known.

Proprioception is the sense of where your body is and how much force it is using. It comes from muscles and joints, and it is the most reliably calming input available. This is why a firm hug settles a child and a light one does not.

The vestibular sense is balance and head position, from the inner ear. Spinning and swinging are alerting; slow rocking is calming.

Between them they explain most of what works when a child is dysregulated.

To calm a child down

Heavy work, which means pushing, pulling, carrying, squeezing. Carrying the shopping in. Pushing a laundry basket across the floor. Wall presses. Kneading dough. A weighted blanket or being squashed under cushions. Slow rocking. Deep firm pressure rather than light touch.

These are the ones worth having ready before you need them, because a child past their limit cannot be talked down and can often be pressed down.

To wake a child up

Spinning, swinging, jumping, cold water, strong smells, sharp or sour tastes, music with a beat. Useful for the flat late-afternoon stretch, and worth avoiding within an hour of bed.

For general development

Touch: water play, sand, rice or lentil trays, dough, mud, finger paint, textures to sort by feel with eyes shut.

Sight: torches in a dark room, colour sorting, spotting games, shadow play.

Sound: shakers, listening games, naming sounds with eyes closed, silence as a game.

Smell and taste: herbs, spices, cooking, guessing with eyes shut. Cooking is unusually good here because it is several senses at once with a real outcome.

A caution worth stating

Sensory play is enjoyable and genuinely useful for regulation. The stronger claims made for it, that particular sensory programmes improve attention, learning or behaviour in a lasting way, are not well supported by evidence, and commercial versions often go well beyond what the research shows.

Use it because it helps a child settle and because it is good play. That is a sufficient reason and it is one you can actually observe working.

If a child is regularly overwhelmed by ordinary environments, clothing or noise, and it is limiting what the family can do, that is worth raising with someone who can observe them directly.
